nodes.question: What is the environmental impact of traditional practices for handling SPL?
nodes.answer: Traditional practices of depositing SPL contribute to greenhouse gas emissions and increase the amount of waste generated by the aluminum industry.
nodes.paragraph: ORIGINAL RESEARCH ARTICLE End-of-Life Treatment of Spent Potlining from the Aluminum Industry by Low Pressureand Heat CAMILLA SOMMERSETH, PER ANDERS EIDEM, PAVEL STRA NSKY A L TETLIE, HEIKO GAERTNER, SAMUEL SENANU, ELLEN MYRVOLD, EIRIK HAGEN,LORENTZ PETTER LOSSIUS, EGIL SKYBAKMOEN, and ANDERS S RHUUS The environmental footprint of the aluminum industry is a ected by greenhouse gas emissions and the amount of waste generated. Spent potlining (SPL) has traditionally been deposited, but increasing scrutiny is put to this practice. The cost of deposit is also increasing. First cut SPL isthe carbon rich part and are the remaining cathode at end-of-life of an aluminum cell. A methodfor cleaning the rst cut SPL is proposed which involves high temperature and low-pressure treatment for removal of uoride-rich electrolyte remains. This way the carbon rich part of the SPL can become a product which can be reused or secondly used as an energy source, instead ofbeing deposited. 5 19 kg of SPL has been treated for four hours in a furnace at low pressure and high temperature, and a post-treatment carbon purity up to 98 wt pct was found.

nodes.question: What are the direct environmental impacts of electronic healthcare devices (EHDs) attributed to?
nodes.answer: The direct environmental impacts of EHDs are attributed to the life cycle stages including raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life (EOL).
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Purpose There has been a recent proliferation of electronic healthcare devices (EHDs); however, their environmental impacts are not yet fully understood. EHDs have direct environmental impacts attributed to the life cycle stages including raw mate - rial extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life (EOL). In addition to the direct impacts, there are indirect impacts that arise from the use of these devices such as favourable effects on the optimization of healthcare procedures and adverse impacts arising from the additional demand for resources. Methods This critical review aimed to gain insight into the state of the art of environmental impact assessments of EHDs, after which challenges were identified and recommendations provided to move towards comprehensive environmental sustain- ability assessments. The literature review relied on three databases (PubMED, Scopus, and Embase) and specific screening steps, resulting in 17 articles, ten of which applied life cycle assessment. Results and discussion This paper identified methodological challenges in the selected studies and lack of consistency in evaluating the environmental impacts of EHDs. For example, seven studies used device-oriented FU, while others applied a treatment-oriented FU, however, all of which aim to investigate the environmental performance of EHDs.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What challenges exist in understanding the environmental sustainability of electronic healthcare devices (EHDs)?
nodes.answer: The inconsistencies between studies complicate the understanding of the environmental sustainability of EHDs, as impacts are primarily assessed at the product level, often ignoring indirect effects related to healthcare value, such as reduced hospital bed days.
nodes.paragraph: These inconsisten- cies between studies make it hard to understand the environmental sustainability of EHDs. Moreover, the impacts of these devices are mostly considered at the product level and overlook potential indirect impacts associated with the healthcare value delivered by the EHDs (e.g. fewer hospital bed days). Conclusions It is important to consider a wider boundary of healthcare pathway rather than the narrow boundary of the device. This will involve considering both the direct life cycle impacts of the device (e.g. impacts related to production or end-of-life) and the positive and negative effects of using the EHDs at the healthcare pathway level. This would result in comprehensive environmental sustainability assessments of EHDs from a healthcare perspective. Keywords LCA Environmental sustainability Electronic healthcare devices Electronic surgical devices Electronic non-surgical devices Healthcare pathway 1 Introduction Technological revolution has played a crucial role in dif- ferent industries such as manufacturing, financial services, retail, and healthcare sector (Lee et al. 2018). It has led to higher productivity, better customer experience, cost reduc- tion, increased efficiency, and easier communication. In the healthcare sector, technological revolution has had a pro- found impact on service delivery and quality of care.

nodes.answer: The direct environmental impacts of EHDs are attributed to their life cycle stages, including raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life (EOL).

EHDs include but are not limited to glucose test strips, smart health patches, hearing aids, drug-releasing pumps, and electronic surgical tools (Shaw et al. 2016). While there are great opportunities created by the use of EHDs, these devices may also place a large burden on the environment. EHDs have both direct and indirect environ- mental impacts. Direct impacts are attributed to the life cycle stages of the device including raw material extraction, manu - facturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life (EOL). Currently, the healthcare sector mainly relies on a linear supply chain composed of single-use electronic devices (Benedettini 2022 ). This inherently unsustainable production and con - sumption model results in the depletion of natural resources, as well as excessive generation of e-waste (MacNeill et al. 2020).

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is it important to evaluate the environmental sustainability of electronic surgical devices?
nodes.answer: It is important to evaluate the environmental sustainability of these devices because their positive impacts might compensate for the increased environmental damage associated with their life cycle stages.
nodes.paragraph: Environmental strategies within the healthcare sector typically focus on waste reduction in addition to reduction in energy use and emissions (Thiel et al. 2015). For instance, minimizing the use of single-use devices in favour of reus- able alternatives is one of the mitigation strategies created by hospitals (Unger and Landis 2016). In addition to the direct impacts, the indirect impacts arise from the use of these devices, which include favour - able effects on the optimization of healthcare procedures and adverse impacts arising from the additional demand for resources. For example, advances in electronic surgi - cal devices have introduced new surgical techniques and diagnostic modalities in medical institutions (Gautam and Sahney 2020). These devices have favoured the use of less invasive procedures leading to shorter hospital stays for patients (Yu et al. 2012). Therefore, it is important to have a comprehensive evaluation of the environmental sustainabil- ity of these devices, because these positive impacts might compensate for the increased environmental damage associ- ated with the life cycle stages (Frag o-Marques and Ozben 2022). nodes.answer: The direct and indirect environmental impacts of waste management include land occupation, resource depletion, global warming, water pollution, and cytotoxic effects from air emissions.

nodes.question: What is the environmental impact of ironing cotton in terms of energy consumption and waste generation?
nodes.answer: In the use phase of ironing cotton, 0.03 kW h of energy is consumed. Additionally, 0.25 kg of waste is generated during the incineration process.

nodes.question: What are some of the severe environmental impacts caused by the conventional economic model characterized by resource extraction, production, and disposal?
nodes.answer: The conventional economic model has been causing severe environmental impacts such as generating 92 million tons of textile waste annually worldwide, with a significant portion ending up in landfills.

nodes.question: What environmental impacts are associated with the manufacturing process of acrylic fibre?
nodes.answer: The manufacturing process of acrylic fibre is energy-intensive, generating about 5.5 kg of CO2 equivalent and 0.013 kg of sulphur dioxide per 1 kg of fibre produced. Additionally, the use of arsenic, chromium, cadmium, and zinc can lead to carcinogenic problems.
